eyebrow: Chips and Semiconductors · 晶片與半導體
lead_en: Chips are in almost everything we use, and Taiwan is famous for making them. But what is inside a chip? Zoom from sand to silicon to switches smaller than a virus, then see how chips are stacked for AI.
lead_zh: 我們用的東西幾乎都有晶片，台灣也以製造晶片聞名。可是晶片裡到底有什麼？從沙子、矽，一路放大到比病毒還小的開關，再看看 AI 晶片怎麼疊在一起。

intro.en: Every lesson starts with a question you might hear in the news or at the dinner table. A 3D model shows the answer, one idea at a time, and an English reading explains it, with Chinese a tap away.
intro.zh: 每一課都從一個新聞裡、餐桌上會聽到的問題開始：先用 3D 模型看答案，一課只講清楚一個道理；再讀一篇英文短文把它說明白，中文翻譯隨點隨看。

intro.en: The lessons are grouped into three units: what a semiconductor is, how chips are made, and the chips behind AI. When a lesson touches an idea already explained in How Things Work, such as solar panels or computer memory, it links there instead of explaining it twice.
intro.zh: 課程分成三個單元：半導體是什麼、晶片怎麼做出來、AI 時代的晶片。遇到「萬物原理」已經講過的東西，例如太陽能板、電腦記憶體，就直接連過去，不重講一次。

intro.en: Every number is checked against a source listed at the bottom of each lesson. Company names appear only to explain how chips are made, never as advice about stocks or investing.
intro.zh: 每一個數字都查證過，出處列在每課最下方。提到公司名稱只是為了說明晶片怎麼做，不談股票，也不做任何投資建議。

units.blurb_en: Why silicon conducts only a little, how a pinch of other atoms changes that, and how a switch with no moving parts runs every computer.
units.blurb_zh: 矽為什麼只導一點點電、加一點點別的原子怎麼改變它，以及沒有任何會動零件的開關怎麼讓電腦運作。

lessons.title: What Is a Semiconductor?
lessons.blurb_en: Copper conducts, glass does not, and silicon is in between. Test all three in 3D, then zoom into silicon's atoms and add a pinch of phosphorus or boron to see how a few atoms change everything.
lessons.blurb_zh: 銅會導電、玻璃不會，矽介於兩者之間。在 3D 裡測試三種材料，再放大到矽的原子，加一點點磷或硼，看幾個原子怎麼改變一切。
lessons.big_idea_en: A semiconductor conducts electricity better than an insulator but far worse than a metal, and its conductivity can be tuned. Swap just a few atoms in pure silicon for phosphorus or boron, and you decide whether it conducts, and how well.
lessons.big_idea_zh: 半導體的導電能力比絕緣體好、比金屬差得多，而且可以「調」：在純矽裡把極少數原子換成磷或硼，就能決定它導不導電、導得多好。

lab.how_en: Drag to turn the model, and scroll or pinch to zoom. In Three materials, the same battery and LED test copper, glass, and silicon. Choose what to add to the silicon and how much, and watch the LED. Then switch to Inside silicon to see why: every silicon atom holds hands with four neighbors, and phosphorus or boron changes that.
lab.how_zh: 拖曳可以旋轉模型，滾輪或雙指可以縮放。「三種材料」用同一顆電池和 LED 測試銅、玻璃和矽；選擇矽裡要加什麼、加多少，看 LED 會不會亮。再切換到「矽的原子」看原因：每個矽原子都和四個鄰居牽手，加進磷或硼就改變了這件事。

paras: Look around your home. The phone in your hand, the TV remote, the rice cooker that beeps when dinner is ready, and even the card you tap on the bus all have at least one chip inside. Almost every chip is made mostly of one material: silicon. Silicon is a semiconductor. You hear that word in the news almost every day, especially in Taiwan. But what does it actually mean?

Electricity is a flow of electrons. In a metal such as copper, many electrons are free to move from atom to atom, so copper is a good conductor. In glass or plastic, every electron is held tightly by its atom, so they are insulators. That is why an electric cord has copper inside and plastic outside. A semiconductor is in between. Pure silicon conducts far better than glass, but copper conducts more than a hundred billion times better than pure silicon.

Silicon is the second most common element in Earth's crust, after oxygen, and most sand is mainly silicon joined with oxygen. A silicon atom has four outer electrons, like four hands. In a silicon crystal, each atom holds hands with four neighbors and shares a pair of electrons with each one. With every hand busy, almost no electrons are free to move. That is why pure silicon is such a poor conductor.

Here is the clever part. Engineers swap a few silicon atoms for atoms of another element. This is called doping. A phosphorus atom has five outer electrons. Four of them hold hands with silicon neighbors, and the fifth is left over, free to move. Silicon with extra free electrons is called n-type, for negative. If just one silicon atom in a million is swapped for phosphorus, the silicon conducts more than a million times better.

Boron does the opposite. A boron atom has only three outer electrons, so one of its hands is empty. That empty place is called a hole. A nearby electron can jump into the hole, but it leaves a new hole behind, so the hole moves, like an empty seat moving along a row as each person shifts over. Silicon with holes is called p-type, for positive. Electrons and holes are also what make a solar panel work.

A chip is a thin, flat piece of silicon with billions of tiny n-type and p-type regions, joined by very thin metal wires. Because engineers can choose exactly where the silicon conducts and how well, they can build switches with no moving parts that turn on and off billions of times every second. Next time you hear the word semiconductor, you will know what it means: a material that conducts a little, and that we can tune.
paras_zh: 看看你家：你手上的手機、電視遙控器、晚餐煮好會嗶嗶叫的電子鍋，連搭公車時嗶一下的卡片，裡面都至少有一顆晶片。幾乎每一顆晶片，主要都是用同一種材料做的：矽。矽是一種半導體。這個詞幾乎每天都出現在新聞裡，在台灣更是如此。可是它到底是什麼意思？
電就是電子的流動。在銅這樣的金屬裡，很多電子可以在原子之間自由移動，所以銅是良好的導體。玻璃或塑膠裡，每個電子都被自己的原子緊緊抓住，所以它們是絕緣體。這就是電線裡面是銅、外面包塑膠的原因。半導體介於兩者之間：純矽導電比玻璃好得多，但銅的導電能力是純矽的一千億倍以上。
矽是地殼裡第二多的元素，僅次於氧；大部分的沙子，主要就是矽和氧結合成的。一個矽原子外圈有四個電子，就像四隻手。在矽晶體裡，每個原子和四個鄰居牽手，和每個鄰居共用一對電子。所有的手都在忙，幾乎沒有電子能自由移動，所以純矽很不會導電。
聰明的地方來了：工程師把少數矽原子換成別種元素的原子，這叫做「摻雜」。磷原子外圈有五個電子：四個和旁邊的矽牽手，第五個多出來，可以自由移動。多了自由電子的矽叫做 N 型，N 代表負（negative）。只要每 100 萬個矽原子裡有 1 個換成磷，矽的導電能力就會變成原來的 100 萬倍以上。
硼正好相反。硼原子外圈只有三個電子，所以有一隻手是空的，這個空位叫做「電洞」。旁邊的電子可以跳進電洞，卻在原來的地方留下新的電洞，所以電洞會移動，就像一排座位上的人一個接一個往旁邊挪，空位子就跟著移動。有電洞的矽叫做 P 型，P 代表正（positive）。太陽能板能發電，靠的也是電子和電洞。
晶片是一片又薄又平的矽，上面有幾十億個極小的 N 型和 P 型區域，用極細的金屬線連起來。因為工程師能精確決定矽的哪裡導電、導得多好，就能做出沒有任何會動零件的開關，每秒開關幾十億次。下次你聽到「半導體」這個詞，就知道它的意思了：一種會導一點點電、而且我們可以調整的材料。
questions: Why does copper conduct electricity well, while glass does not?
Why is pure silicon a poor conductor?
What happens when a little phosphorus is added to silicon?
answers: In copper, many electrons are free to move. In glass, every electron is held tightly by its atom.
Each silicon atom holds hands with four neighbors and shares its four outer electrons, so almost no electrons are free to move.
Each phosphorus atom brings a fifth electron that is free to move, so the silicon conducts much better. It becomes n-type silicon.

home.en: How many chips are in your home?
home.lead_en: Tick the things your family has and set how many. We filled in a sample home; change it to match yours.
home.lead_zh: 勾選你家有的東西、填上數量。我們先填了一個範例家庭，改成你家的樣子吧。
home.note_en: These are low estimates, not exact counts. Only two numbers come from published sources: a 2025 teardown of one smartphone identified 38 chips, so we count 30 per phone, and the U.S. Commerce Department said in 2021 that an average electric car has about 2,000 chips, roughly double a regular car, so we count 1,000 per car. For an appliance with buttons, we count just one chip, the tiny computer called a microcontroller that reads the buttons. For computers, tablets, TVs, and the like, the numbers are our own low guesses. Most homes really have more.
home.note_zh: 這些是保守的估計，不是精確的數字。只有兩個數字有公開出處：2025 年一支智慧型手機拆解後認出 38 顆晶片，所以我們每支手機只算 30 顆；美國商務部 2021 年說，電動車平均約有 2,000 顆晶片，大約是一般汽車的兩倍，所以每輛車算 1,000 顆。有按鍵的家電，我們只算一顆：讀取按鍵的小電腦「微控制器」。電腦、平板、電視這些，是我們自己保守的猜測。大部分家庭實際上更多。

culture_cards.title_en: Sand, a word, a park, and your first chip
culture_cards.title_zh: 沙子、一個詞、一座園區、你的第一顆晶片
culture_cards.lead_en: Four short stories behind a word you hear in the news.
culture_cards.lead_zh: 新聞裡常聽到的這個詞，背後的四個小故事。

cards.body_en: Silicon makes up about 28% of Earth's crust by mass, and most sand is mainly silicon dioxide. But chips are not made from beach sand directly. Quartz is heated with carbon in an electric furnace to make silicon that is about 98% pure, and then it is cleaned chemically until fewer than one atom in a billion is unwanted.
cards.body_zh: 矽約占地殼質量的 28%，大部分的沙子主要是二氧化矽。但晶片不是直接拿沙灘的沙來做：先把石英和碳一起放進電爐加熱，得到純度約 98% 的矽，再用化學方法提純，直到不要的原子少於十億分之一。

cards.body_en: According to historians, Alessandro Volta, the Italian scientist who built the first battery, called some materials “semiconducting” as early as 1782. In 1910, Josef Weiss used the German word Halbleiter, “half conductor,” in its modern sense. Chinese uses the same idea: 半 (half) + 導體 (conductor). “Half” does not mean it conducts half the time. It means its conductivity sits between a metal's and an insulator's.
cards.body_zh: 據歷史學者的研究，發明第一顆電池的義大利科學家伏打，早在 1782 年就用「半導電」形容某些材料。1910 年，魏斯用德文 Halbleiter（「半導體」）表達今天的意思。中文用的是同一個想法：半＋導體。「半」不是說它一半時間導電，而是說它的導電能力介於金屬和絕緣體之間。

cards.body_en: Hsinchu Science Park officially opened on December 15, 1980, as Taiwan's first science park. Its administration says more than 600 companies have been approved to join and more than 160,000 people work there. In 2021, integrated circuits, the industry that makes chips, was its biggest industry by number of companies.
cards.body_zh: 新竹科學園區在 1980 年 12 月 15 日正式成立，是台灣第一個科學園區。依竹科管理局的資料，核准進駐的廠商超過 600 家，就業人數超過 16 萬人。2021 年，積體電路（也就是做晶片的產業）是園區裡廠商家數最多的產業。

cards.k: Your First Chip · 你的第一顆晶片
cards.zh: 世界第一顆晶片，和你的第一顆
cards.body_en: On September 12, 1958, Jack Kilby of Texas Instruments showed the first integrated circuit, built on a small piece of germanium. In 1960, a team at Fairchild made the first working chips on silicon. Kilby later shared the 2000 Nobel Prize in Physics. In Taiwan, your own first chip may be your health insurance card: chip cards fully replaced the old paper cards on January 1, 2004.
cards.body_zh: 1958 年 9 月 12 日，德州儀器的基爾比展示了第一個積體電路，做在一小片鍺上。1960 年，快捷半導體的團隊做出第一批能運作的矽晶片。基爾比後來獲得 2000 年諾貝爾物理獎（與他人共享）。在台灣，你自己的第一顆晶片可能就是健保卡：2004 年 1 月 1 日起，晶片卡全面取代了舊的紙卡。

myths.myth_en: A semiconductor is half conductor and half insulator.
myths.myth_zh: 半導體就是一半導電、一半不導電。
myths.fact_en: The whole material conducts, just much less than a metal. “Semi” means its conductivity is in between, and it can be changed by adding other atoms, by heat, or by light.
myths.fact_zh: 整塊材料都會導電，只是比金屬差得多。「半」是說它的導電能力介於中間，而且加入別的原子、加熱或照光都能改變它。

myths.myth_en: Chips are made of metal.
myths.myth_zh: 晶片是金屬做的。
myths.fact_en: A chip is mostly silicon, which is not a metal. Very thin metal lines, usually copper or aluminum, connect its parts, and the shiny metal legs belong to the package that protects it.
myths.fact_zh: 晶片主要是矽，矽不是金屬。極細的金屬線（通常是銅或鋁）把裡面的元件連起來；看得到的亮晶晶金屬腳，屬於保護它的外殼（封裝）。

myths.myth_en: Beach sand can go straight into a chip factory.
myths.myth_zh: 沙灘上的沙直接就能拿去做晶片。
myths.fact_en: Quartz must first be turned into silicon in a furnace, then purified until fewer than one atom in a billion is unwanted, and grown into a single large crystal before chips can be made.
myths.fact_zh: 要先在電爐裡把石英變成矽，再提純到不要的原子少於十億分之一，還要長成一整塊單晶，才能拿來做晶片。

myths.myth_en: Silicon and silicone are the same thing.
myths.myth_zh: 矽（silicon）和矽膠（silicone）是同一種東西。
myths.fact_en: Silicon is an element, a hard, shiny, blue-gray solid. Silicone is a soft, rubbery material, used for things like phone cases and baking molds, made of silicon joined with oxygen, carbon, and hydrogen. Silicon Valley is named after silicon chips.
myths.fact_zh: 矽是一種元素，是堅硬、帶藍灰色光澤的固體。矽膠（silicone，又叫矽利康）是軟軟的、像橡膠的材料，用來做手機殼、烘焙模具，由矽和氧、碳、氫組成。矽谷的「矽」指的是矽晶片。

tricks.title_zh: 導體、絕緣體，半導體在中間
tricks.body_en: Copper lets electrons go, glass holds them tight, and silicon is in between.
tricks.body_zh: 銅放電子走，玻璃把電子抓緊，矽在中間。

tricks.body_en: Each silicon atom shares four pairs of electrons with its neighbors, so almost none are free.
tricks.body_zh: 每個矽原子和鄰居共用四對電子，所以幾乎沒有自由電子。

tricks.body_en: Phosphorus (5) adds a free electron: n-type. Boron (3) leaves a hole: p-type.
tricks.body_zh: 磷（5 個）多出自由電子：N 型。硼（3 個）留下電洞：P 型。

tricks.body_en: Swap one atom in a million, and silicon conducts over a million times better.
tricks.body_zh: 每 100 萬個原子換 1 個，導電能力就變成 100 萬倍以上。

safety.en: Use only small dry-cell batteries, such as AA or AAA. Never put wires, clips, or any metal into a wall outlet.
safety.zh: 只用三號、四號這類小型乾電池。電線、夾子或任何金屬都絕不能插進牆上的插座。

safety.en: Never connect the two ends of a battery directly with a wire, foil, or a paper clip. That is a short circuit, and the wire and battery can get hot.
safety.zh: 絕不要用電線、鋁箔或迴紋針直接連接電池的兩端。那是短路，電線和電池會發燙。

safety.en: Keep button batteries away from young children. A swallowed button battery is a medical emergency.
safety.zh: 鈕扣電池要遠離幼兒；誤吞鈕扣電池要立刻就醫。

safety.en: Never take apart a phone or computer to look for its chips. The lithium battery inside can catch fire if it is bent or punctured.
safety.zh: 絕不要拆開手機或電腦找晶片：裡面的鋰電池被折到或刺破，可能會起火。

safety.en: Do not put coins, clips, or batteries in your mouth, and wash your hands after the activity.
safety.zh: 硬幣、夾子、電池都不要放進嘴裡；活動結束後要洗手。

materials.en: A holder for two AA batteries, with two AA batteries
materials.zh: 兩顆三號電池和電池盒

materials.en: A red LED and a 100-ohm resistor (or an LED with a built-in resistor)
materials.zh: 一顆紅色 LED 和一個 100 歐姆電阻（或內建電阻的 LED）

materials.en: Three wires with alligator clips
materials.zh: 三條附鱷魚夾的電線

materials.en: Things to test: a pencil lead, a paper clip, an eraser, a coin, aluminum foil, a plastic ruler, a wooden chopstick, a glass marble
materials.zh: 要測的東西：鉛筆芯、迴紋針、橡皮擦、硬幣、鋁箔、塑膠尺、竹筷、玻璃彈珠

steps.en: Connect the battery holder, the resistor, and the LED in a loop, but leave one gap with two free clips. The LED's longer leg goes toward the + side.
steps.zh: 把電池盒、電阻和 LED 接成一圈，但留一個缺口，缺口兩邊各是一個鱷魚夾。LED 比較長的腳接「＋」那一邊。

steps.en: Touch the two free clips together. The LED should light up. If it does not, turn the LED around.
steps.zh: 把兩個鱷魚夾碰在一起，LED 應該會亮；如果不亮，就把 LED 反過來接。

steps.en: Before each test, predict whether the LED will light. Then clip both ends of the object and write down bright, dim, or dark.
steps.zh: 每次測試之前先猜猜看會不會亮，再用兩個夾子夾住東西的兩端，記錄「亮、微亮、不亮」。

steps.en: Sort your objects into conductors and insulators. Which ones surprised you? Pencil lead is not a metal, so why does it conduct?
steps.zh: 把東西分成導體和絕緣體。哪些結果讓你意外？鉛筆芯不是金屬，為什麼會導電？

activities.tip_en: Coins and foil can have paint or plastic coatings that block the current, so clip a clean, shiny spot. Pencil lead is graphite, a form of carbon that conducts electricity.
activities.tip_zh: 硬幣和鋁箔表面可能有漆或塑膠膜擋住電流，要夾在乾淨、亮亮的地方。鉛筆芯是石墨，一種會導電的碳。

materials.en: Bean bags or balls of paper: about one per student, plus a few extra
materials.zh: 沙包或揉成球的紙：大約每人一個，再多準備幾個

materials.en: Two signs: “−” and “+”, taped to opposite walls
materials.zh: 兩張牌子：「−」和「＋」，貼在教室兩邊的牆上

materials.en: Two colored caps or stickers for the “phosphorus” and “boron” students
materials.zh: 兩頂彩色帽子或貼紙，給扮演「磷」和「硼」的同學

steps.en: Stand in rows between the two signs and hold hands with the people beside you. Each pair of joined hands holds one bean bag: a shared electron. Every hand is busy, so no bean bag can move. This is pure silicon.
steps.zh: 在兩張牌子之間排成幾排，和旁邊的同學牽手。每一對牽著的手夾著一個沙包，代表共用的電子。所有的手都在忙，沒有沙包能移動：這就是純矽。

steps.en: One student puts on the phosphorus cap and holds an extra bean bag under one arm. That electron has no hand to hold, so roll it along the floor toward the + sign. This is n-type.
steps.zh: 一位同學戴上「磷」的帽子，腋下多夾一個沙包。這個電子沒有手可以牽，就讓它沿著地板滾向「＋」：這就是 N 型。

steps.en: Now one student puts on the boron cap. One pair of their joined hands holds no bean bag: that is a hole. The pair on the − side passes its bean bag into the empty hands, which leaves its own hands empty. Keep passing.
steps.zh: 換一位同學戴上「硼」的帽子，他有一對牽著的手沒有沙包：這就是電洞。靠「−」那一邊的一對手，把沙包傳進空著的手裡，自己的手就空了。一直傳下去。

steps.en: Talk about it: the bean bags moved toward +, but the empty hands moved toward −. Why do we say holes move the opposite way from electrons?
steps.zh: 討論：沙包往「＋」移動，空著的手卻往「−」移動。為什麼我們說電洞移動的方向和電子相反？

activities.tip_en: Go slowly and call out each pass. Watching the empty hands travel is the whole point.
activities.tip_zh: 慢慢來，每傳一次就喊出來。看著「空手」一路移動，就是這個活動的重點。

sources.zh: 矽占地殼質量 27.7%，僅次於氧；沙子是二氧化矽；矽是把沙或石英和碳放進電爐加熱製成

lessons.title: What Does a Transistor Do?
lessons.blurb_en: A transistor is a switch with no moving parts. Turn up the gate voltage and watch a channel of electrons appear in 3D, then wire two switches together to make AND, OR, and the first step of adding.
lessons.blurb_zh: 電晶體是沒有任何會動零件的開關。在 3D 裡調高閘極電壓，看電子的通道長出來；再把兩個開關接在一起，做出「且」「或」和加法的第一步。
lessons.big_idea_en: A transistor is a switch controlled by electricity. A small voltage on its gate opens a channel of electrons, so current can flow; take the voltage away, and the channel closes. On means 1 and off means 0, and billions of these switches, wired together, can do math.
lessons.big_idea_zh: 電晶體是用電控制的開關：閘極加一點電壓，就打開一條電子的通道讓電流通過；拿掉電壓，通道就關上。開代表 1、關代表 0，幾十億個這樣的開關接在一起，就能算數學。

lab.how_en: Drag to turn the model, and scroll or pinch to zoom. In One transistor, slide the gate voltage up and watch electrons gather under the gate to make a channel between the source and the drain. Then switch to Switches that add, turn inputs A and B on and off, and see which lights come on when two transistors are wired in a row or side by side.
lab.how_zh: 拖曳可以旋轉模型，滾輪或雙指可以縮放。在「一顆電晶體」把閘極電壓往上拉，看電子聚到閘極下面，在源極和汲極之間鋪出通道。再切換到「會算數的開關」，打開、關掉輸入 A 和 B，看兩顆電晶體串在一起或並排時，哪一顆燈會亮。

The voltages are only for illustration. The electrons are slowed down enormously so you can watch them; a real chip's clock ticks more than three billion times every second.

paras: In the last lesson, you saw that engineers can make silicon conduct by adding a pinch of phosphorus or boron. Now comes the amazing part. A chip uses n-type and p-type silicon to build tiny switches called transistors, often billions of them. A transistor has no moving parts, yet it can turn a current on and off billions of times every second. Every app, photo, and game on your phone depends on these switches.

Most transistors in a chip work like this. Two n-type regions, called the source and the drain, sit in a piece of p-type silicon. Electrons would gladly flow from the source to the drain, but the p-type silicon between them blocks the way. Above that gap is the gate, a layer that conducts, separated from the silicon by a very thin layer of insulator.

When a small positive voltage is put on the gate, it pulls electrons into a thin layer just under the insulator. This layer, called a channel, joins the source to the drain, and current flows. The switch is on. Take the voltage away, and the channel disappears, so the switch is off. The gate never touches the current. It controls the current from the other side of the insulator.

A switch has only two states, on and off, and computers use them to stand for 1 and 0. With 0s and 1s, a computer can write any number, just as we write any number with the ten digits 0 to 9. This way of counting is called binary. In binary, the numbers one, two, three, and four are written 1, 10, 11, and 100.

How can switches do math? Put two transistors in a row, and current flows only if both are on. That is called an AND gate. Put them side by side, and current flows if either one is on. That is an OR gate. A few gates together can add. In binary, 1 + 1 = 10: the sum is 0, and a 1 is carried to the next place, just like carrying a 1 when you add 5 + 5.

The first transistor was built at Bell Labs in the United States in 1947, and its three inventors shared the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1956. In 1971, Intel's first microprocessor, the 4004, had 2,300 transistors. In 2024, Apple announced a chip with 28 billion. Each one is a switch, flipping on and off and adding up our world one 1 and 0 at a time.
paras_zh: 上一課看到，工程師在矽裡加一點點磷或硼，就能讓它導電。接下來才是最神奇的部分：晶片用 N 型和 P 型矽做出極小的開關，叫做「電晶體」，數量常常有幾十億顆。電晶體沒有任何會動的零件，卻能每秒把電流開關幾十億次。手機裡的每個 App、每張照片、每個遊戲，都靠這些開關。
晶片裡大部分的電晶體是這樣運作的：一塊 P 型矽上有兩塊 N 型區域，叫做「源極」和「汲極」。電子很樂意從源極流到汲極，可是中間的 P 型矽擋住了路。在這段空隙上方是「閘極」：一層會導電的材料，和矽之間隔著一層非常薄的絕緣層。
在閘極加上一點正電壓，它就把電子吸到絕緣層正下方，形成薄薄的一層。這一層叫做「通道」，把源極和汲極連起來，電流就流過去了：開關打開。把電壓拿掉，通道就消失，開關關上。閘極從來不碰電流，而是隔著絕緣層控制它。
開關只有兩種狀態：開和關，電腦就用它們代表 1 和 0。只用 0 和 1，電腦就能寫出任何數字，就像我們用 0 到 9 十個數字寫出任何數一樣。這種數法叫做「二進位」。在二進位裡，一、二、三、四寫成 1、10、11、100。
開關怎麼算數學？把兩顆電晶體排成一串，兩顆都開，電流才過得去，這叫「且閘」（AND gate）。把它們並排，只要有一顆開，電流就過得去，這叫「或閘」（OR gate）。幾個閘組合起來就能做加法。在二進位裡，1＋1＝10：這一位是 0，再進 1 到下一位，就像算 5＋5 時要進位一樣。
第一顆電晶體 1947 年在美國的貝爾實驗室做出來，三位發明人在 1956 年共同獲得諾貝爾物理獎。1971 年，英特爾第一顆微處理器 4004 有 2,300 顆電晶體；2024 年，蘋果發表了一顆有 280 億顆電晶體的晶片。每一顆都是一個開關，開開關關，用一個個 1 和 0 算出我們的世界。

parts_head.eyebrow: Try It in the Model · 在模型裡試試

parts.text_en: With no voltage on the gate, the p-type silicon blocks the way. No channel, no current.
parts.text_zh: 閘極沒有電壓，P 型矽把路擋住：沒有通道，就沒有電流。

parts.text_en: Turn the gate voltage up. Watch the holes get pushed away and a channel of electrons appear.
parts.text_zh: 把閘極電壓調高：看電洞被推開，一條電子的通道長出來。

parts.text_en: Current has to pass through both transistors, so the light needs A and B.
parts.text_zh: 電流要通過兩顆電晶體，所以 A 和 B 都要開，燈才亮。

parts.text_en: Current can take either path, so the light needs only A or B.
parts.text_zh: 電流可以走任何一條路，所以 A 或 B 有一個開，燈就亮。

lessons.parts_note_en: Real chips usually pair this kind of transistor with a p-channel one that turns on with the opposite voltage, so that almost no current is wasted while they wait. The idea is the same: a gate that opens and closes a channel.
lessons.parts_note_zh: 真的晶片通常把這種電晶體和「P 通道」電晶體配成一對（相反的電壓才打開），等待時幾乎不浪費電流。道理一樣：閘極打開、關上一條通道。

links.note_zh: N 型矽為什麼有自由電子、P 型矽為什麼有電洞：每顆電晶體都用這兩種材料做成。

count.note_zh: 電晶體數量是廠商公布的數字。Blackwell 是兩片矽接在一起、當成一顆晶片使用。

items.en: Source, drain, and gate.
items.zh: 源極、汲極、閘極。

items.en: On means 1 and off means 0.
items.zh: 開代表 1，關代表 0。

items.en: The first microprocessor sold by Intel.
items.zh: 英特爾推出的第一顆微處理器。

items.zh: 是 4004 的一千萬倍以上。

culture_cards.eyebrow: Transistor Stories · 電晶體的故事
culture_cards.title_en: A Christmas present, a name, a law, and a record
culture_cards.title_zh: 一份聖誕禮物、一個名字、一條定律、一項紀錄
culture_cards.lead_en: Four short stories about the switch inside everything.
culture_cards.lead_zh: 關於「萬物裡的開關」的四個小故事。

cards.body_en: On December 16, 1947, John Bardeen and Walter Brattain at Bell Labs in the United States made the first working transistor: two gold contacts pressed onto a piece of germanium. They showed it to lab officials on December 23, and their group leader, William Shockley, called it a magnificent Christmas present. The three men shared the 1956 Nobel Prize in Physics.
cards.body_zh: 1947 年 12 月 16 日，美國貝爾實驗室的巴丁和布拉頓做出第一顆能運作的電晶體：兩個金接點壓在一小塊鍺上。他們在 12 月 23 日展示給實驗室主管看，小組領導人蕭克利說這是「一份很棒的聖誕禮物」。三人在 1956 年共同獲得諾貝爾物理獎。

cards.body_en: Engineer John Pierce named it. Vacuum tubes had a property called transconductance, and the new device had transresistance, so Pierce began the name with “trans-” and ended it like the varistor and the thermistor, other new parts of the time. Bell Labs announced the transistor to the public on June 30, 1948. The Chinese name, 電晶體, means “electric crystal.”
cards.body_zh: 命名的是工程師皮爾斯。真空管有一種性質叫 transconductance，新元件則有 transresistance，所以他用「trans-」開頭，結尾學當時的新零件 varistor、thermistor。貝爾實驗室在 1948 年 6 月 30 日向大眾公布電晶體。中文「電晶體」，字面上就是「電的晶體」。

cards.body_en: In 1965, Gordon Moore predicted that the number of parts on a chip would double every year. In 1975 he changed it to every two years. From the 4004's 2,300 transistors in 1971 to 28 billion in Apple's M4 in 2024 is more than ten million times as many.
cards.body_zh: 1965 年，摩爾預測晶片上的元件數量每年會加倍；1975 年他改成每兩年加倍。從 1971 年 4004 的 2,300 顆，到 2024 年蘋果 M4 的 280 億顆，增加了一千萬倍以上。

cards.body_en: In 2018, the Computer History Museum reported an estimate that about 13 sextillion transistors had been made since 1947. That is 13 followed by 21 zeros, which makes the transistor the most frequently manufactured human artifact in history. Almost all of them are MOS transistors, the kind in this lesson.
cards.body_zh: 2018 年，美國電腦歷史博物館引用分析師的估計：從 1947 年到當時，人類大約做了 1.3 × 10²² 顆電晶體，也就是 13 後面接 21 個 0。這讓電晶體成為人類史上製造數量最多的東西，而且幾乎全是這一課講的 MOS 電晶體。

myths.myth_en: A transistor has tiny moving parts that click on and off.
myths.myth_zh: 電晶體裡有會喀噠開關的小零件。
myths.fact_en: Nothing moves except electrons. A voltage on the gate makes a channel of electrons appear or disappear.
myths.fact_zh: 除了電子，什麼都沒有動。閘極上的電壓讓一條電子的通道出現或消失。

myths.myth_en: Inside a computer, numbers are stored with the digits 0 to 9.
myths.myth_zh: 電腦裡的數字是用 0 到 9 存的。
myths.fact_en: Inside the chip, every number is stored in binary, using only 0s and 1s, because a switch has only two states.
myths.fact_zh: 晶片裡每個數字都用二進位存，只有 0 和 1，因為開關只有兩種狀態。

myths.myth_en: Transistors were first made for computers.
myths.myth_zh: 電晶體一開始是為電腦做的。
myths.fact_en: In the United States, the first transistor products were a hearing aid in 1952 and the Regency TR-1 pocket radio in 1954.
myths.fact_zh: 在美國，最早用電晶體的產品是 1952 年的助聽器，和 1954 年的口袋收音機 Regency TR-1。

myths.myth_en: When a transistor is off, its electrons disappear.
myths.myth_zh: 電晶體關掉時，電子就不見了。
myths.fact_en: The electrons are still in the source and the drain. Off only means there is no channel joining them.
myths.fact_zh: 電子還在源極和汲極裡；「關」只是表示沒有通道把它們連起來。

tricks.body_en: A small voltage on the gate pulls in electrons and opens the way.
tricks.body_zh: 閘極加一點電壓，把電子吸過來，路就通了。

tricks.body_en: Two states are all a computer needs to write any number.
tricks.body_zh: 電腦只要兩種狀態，就能寫出任何數字。

tricks.title_en: In a row is AND, side by side is OR
tricks.body_en: A row needs both switches; side by side needs just one.
tricks.body_zh: 串在一起要兩個都開；並排只要一個開。

tricks.body_en: In binary, write 0 and carry the 1, just like 5 + 5.
tricks.body_zh: 二進位裡寫 0、進 1，就像 5＋5。

safety.en: Use only small dry-cell batteries, such as AA or AAA. Never put wires, clips, or any metal into a wall outlet.
safety.zh: 只用三號、四號這類小型乾電池。電線、夾子或任何金屬都絕不能插進牆上的插座。

safety.en: Never connect the two ends of a battery directly with a wire or a paper clip. That is a short circuit, and it can get hot.
safety.zh: 絕不要用電線或迴紋針直接連接電池兩端。那是短路，會發燙。

safety.en: Ask an adult to make the holes in the cardboard for the paper-clip switches.
safety.zh: 迴紋針開關要在紙板上打洞時，請大人幫忙。

safety.en: Keep button batteries away from young children. A swallowed button battery is a medical emergency.
safety.zh: 鈕扣電池要遠離幼兒；誤吞鈕扣電池要立刻就醫。

safety.en: Never take apart a phone or computer to look for its transistors. The lithium battery inside can catch fire if it is bent or punctured.
safety.zh: 絕不要拆開手機或電腦找電晶體：裡面的鋰電池被折到或刺破，可能會起火。

activities.title_en: Build AND and OR with Two Switches
activities.title_zh: 用兩個開關做出「且」和「或」

materials.en: A holder for two AA batteries, with two AA batteries
materials.zh: 兩顆三號電池和電池盒

materials.en: A red LED and a 100-ohm resistor (or an LED with a built-in resistor)
materials.zh: 一顆紅色 LED 和一個 100 歐姆電阻（或內建電阻的 LED）

materials.en: Two switches, or make each one from a paper clip and two brass paper fasteners on cardboard
materials.zh: 兩個開關，或用迴紋針和兩個雙腳釘在紙板上各做一個

materials.en: Five wires with alligator clips
materials.zh: 五條附鱷魚夾的電線

steps.en: Make a loop of the battery, the resistor, the LED, and one switch. Check that the switch turns the LED on and off. The LED's longer leg goes toward the + side.
steps.zh: 把電池、電阻、LED 和一個開關接成一圈，確認開關能讓 LED 亮和熄。LED 比較長的腳接「＋」那一邊。

steps.en: Put the two switches in a row. Try all four ways to set them, and fill in a table: A, B, light on or off.
steps.zh: 把兩個開關串在一起。試試四種開關組合，填一張表：A、B、燈亮或不亮。

steps.en: Rebuild the circuit with the two switches side by side, and fill in a second table.
steps.zh: 改成兩個開關並排，再填第二張表。

steps.en: Compare the tables. Which one is AND, and which is OR? Think of a door with two locks, and a room with two doors.
steps.zh: 比較兩張表：哪一張是「且」、哪一張是「或」？想想「一扇門有兩道鎖」和「一個房間有兩扇門」。

activities.tip_en: Draw the circuit before you build it, and open the switches whenever you move a wire.
activities.tip_zh: 接線前先把電路畫出來；每次移動電線時，都先把開關打開（斷開）。

materials.en: Your hands
materials.zh: 你的雙手

materials.en: Paper and a pencil
materials.zh: 紙和鉛筆

steps.en: Give each finger a value: thumb 1, pointer 2, middle 4, ring 8, little finger 16. A raised finger is a 1, and a folded finger is a 0.
steps.zh: 每根手指一個值：拇指 1、食指 2、中指 4、無名指 8、小指 16。伸直是 1，彎下是 0。

steps.en: Count from 0 to 31 together, raising fingers to make each number. Write a few numbers in binary, such as 5 = 101.
steps.zh: 全班一起從 0 數到 31，用伸直的手指湊出每個數。把幾個數寫成二進位，例如 5＝101。

steps.en: Add two small numbers with a partner, one on each hand. When two 1s meet in the same place, write 0 and carry 1 to the next finger.
steps.zh: 和同學各用一隻手比一個小數字，把它們加起來：同一位遇到兩個 1，就寫 0、進 1 到下一根手指。

steps.en: Talk about it: one hand counts to 31. How high can two hands, ten fingers, count? (Answer: 1,023.)
steps.zh: 討論：一隻手可以數到 31，兩隻手十根手指能數到多少？（答案：1,023。）

activities.tip_en: The number 4 raises only the middle finger, so many teachers have students turn their hands sideways and laugh about it together.
activities.tip_zh: 數字 4 只伸中指，很多老師會請學生把手轉成側面，大家一起笑一笑就好。

sources.zh: MOS 電晶體構造：P 型基底裡的 N 型源極與汲極；閘極在薄絕緣層上；正電壓形成 N 通道

sources.zh: CMOS 把 N 通道與 P 通道電晶體配成一對

sources.zh: 串聯開關要兩個都開（且）；並聯有一個開就好（或）

sources.en: Half adder: XOR for the sum, AND for the carry
sources.zh: 半加器：和用 XOR、進位用 AND

sources.zh: 摩爾定律：每年加倍（1965），改成每兩年（1975）

sources.zh: 1947 年以來約 1.3 × 10²² 顆電晶體（分析師估計，2018）：人類製造最多的東西

sources.zh: 最早的電晶體消費產品：助聽器（1952）、Regency TR-1 收音機（1954）

sources.en: Clock rate: 3 GHz means three billion cycles per second
sources.zh: 時脈：3 GHz＝每秒 30 億次

sources.en: Recent phone chips run at more than 3.7 GHz (Apple A17 Pro up to 3.78 GHz)
sources.zh: 近年的手機晶片時脈超過 3.7 GHz（蘋果 A17 Pro 最高 3.78 GHz）

sources.en: Taiwan's population at the end of August 2026: 23,224,721 (Ministry of the Interior data)
sources.zh: 台灣 2026 年 8 月底人口 23,224,721 人（內政部資料）

units.blurb_en: From quartz to a shining wafer, drawing circuits with light, and how small a nanometer really is.
units.blurb_zh: 從石英到閃亮的晶圓、用光畫出電路，以及奈米到底有多小。

lessons.title: How Does Sand Become a Chip?
lessons.blurb_en: Follow silicon from a pile of quartz sand to a shining wafer in 3D: melt it, purify it, pull a giant crystal out of a pot of liquid silicon, slice it thin, and cut out hundreds of chips. Then find out how many chips one wafer can hold.
lessons.blurb_zh: 在 3D 裡跟著矽，從一堆石英砂走到閃亮的晶圓：熔煉、提純、從一鍋熔化的矽裡拉出一根大單晶、切成薄片，再切出幾百顆晶片。最後算算一片晶圓能做幾顆晶片。
lessons.big_idea_en: Chips are made from the silicon in sand. It is purified until almost every atom is silicon, grown into one giant crystal, and sliced into thin wafers, and each wafer carries hundreds of chips at once.
lessons.big_idea_zh: 晶片的原料是沙子裡的矽：先提純到幾乎每一個原子都是矽，長成一整根大單晶，再切成薄薄的晶圓；一片晶圓上同時做出幾百顆晶片。

lab.how_en: Drag to turn the model, and scroll or pinch to zoom. Press a step to fly to it and watch it happen, or press Play the whole journey to visit all six in order. The calculator below the reading changes the size of the chips on the last wafer.
lab.how_zh: 拖曳可以旋轉模型，滾輪或雙指可以縮放。按一個步驟，飛過去看它怎麼做；或按「播放全程」，六站依序走一遍。課文下方的計算器可以改變最後那片晶圓上晶片的大小。
lab.overview_en: This is the whole production line. Read it like two lines of text: the back row first, from left to right, then the front row. Choose a step to look closer.
lab.overview_zh: 這是整條生產線。像讀兩行字一樣看：先看後排、由左到右，再看前排。選一個步驟靠近看。

steps.text_en: Most sand is mainly quartz: silicon joined with oxygen. To make silicon, factories usually start with high-purity quartz rock rather than ordinary beach sand.
steps.text_zh: 大部分的沙子主要是石英，也就是矽和氧結合成的。煉矽時，工廠通常用高純度的石英岩，而不是一般沙灘的沙。

steps.text_en: Quartz and carbon are heated in an electric arc furnace. The carbon pulls the oxygen away, leaving silicon. It is about 98 to 99 percent pure, still far too dirty for a chip.
steps.text_zh: 石英和碳一起放進電弧爐加熱，碳把氧帶走，留下矽。純度約 98% 到 99%，對晶片來說還是太髒了。

steps.text_en: The silicon is turned into a liquid chemical, trichlorosilane, and purified. Then it is turned back into silicon on thin rods glowing inside a bell-shaped reactor, and the rods grow thick with polysilicon.
steps.text_zh: 矽先變成一種液體化學品「三氯矽烷」再提純，然後在鐘形反應爐裡發熱的細矽棒上變回矽，矽棒越長越粗，就是多晶矽。

steps.text_en: The pure silicon is melted in a pot. A seed crystal is dipped in and slowly pulled up while it turns. The silicon freezes onto it with every atom lined up the same way: the Czochralski method.
steps.text_zh: 純矽在坩堝裡熔化。把一小塊晶種浸進去，一邊旋轉一邊慢慢往上拉，矽就凝固在晶種上，每個原子都排成同一個方向：這叫柴可拉斯基法。

nums.v_zh: 長約 2 公尺、重數百公斤

steps.text_en: A wire saw slices the ingot into thin disks. The wafers are ground, etched, and polished until they shine like mirrors.
steps.text_zh: 鋼線鋸把晶棒切成薄薄的圓片，再經過研磨、蝕刻、拋光，亮得像鏡子一樣。

steps.text_en: Hundreds of chips are built side by side on each wafer, layer by layer. Each one is tested on the wafer, then the wafer is cut apart and the good chips are packaged.
steps.text_zh: 每片晶圓上一層一層、並排做出幾百顆晶片。先在晶圓上逐顆測試，再切開，把好的晶片封裝起來。

legend.zh: 沙子：大部分是石英，也就是矽和氧結合成的

legend.en: Silver gray: silicon
legend.zh: 銀灰色：矽

legend.en: Orange glow: very hot, or melted
legend.zh: 橘色的光：非常燙，或已經熔化

legend.en: Blue squares: chips on the wafer
legend.zh: 藍色方格：晶圓上的晶片

Each step is sped up to a few seconds. The chips on the last wafer are laid out with the same calculator as the one below the reading.
lab.scale_zh: 這是示意圖，不是真實比例：砂粒放大了，晶棒畫得比真的短很多，晶圓也畫得比 775 微米厚得多；每一步都加快成幾秒鐘。最後那片晶圓上的晶片，用的是和課文下方計算器同一套算法。

paras: A chip begins as something you can find on almost any beach: sand. Most sand is mainly quartz, which is silicon joined with oxygen, and silicon is the second most common element in Earth's crust. But a chip needs silicon so pure and so perfectly arranged that turning sand into a chip is one of the most careful jobs people have ever learned to do.

First, the oxygen has to go. Factories usually start with high-purity quartz rock rather than beach sand. They heat it with carbon in an electric furnace hotter than 2,000 degrees Celsius. The carbon pulls the oxygen away, leaving silicon that is about 98 to 99 percent pure. That sounds pure, but for a chip it is still far too dirty.

Next, the silicon is cleaned with chemistry. It is turned into a liquid called trichlorosilane, purified, and then turned back into silicon on thin rods heated to about 1,150 degrees. The rods slowly grow thick. The result is called polysilicon, and for chips it is at least 99.99999999 percent pure. That is ten nines in a row.

Polysilicon is made of many tiny crystals, but a chip needs one single crystal. So the silicon is melted at 1,414 degrees. A small seed crystal is dipped into the liquid and slowly pulled up while it turns. The silicon freezes onto the seed with every atom lined up the same way, growing into a long, shiny ingot that can be about two meters long. This is called the Czochralski method, after the Polish scientist who invented it in 1916.

Next, a wire saw slices the ingot into thin disks called wafers. The wafers are ground, etched, and polished until they shine like mirrors. The main size used for advanced chips today is 300 millimeters across, usually called a 12-inch wafer, and it is only about 775 micrometers thick, less than one millimeter.

Finally, hundreds of chips are built side by side on each wafer, layer by layer, as you will see in the next lesson. Every chip is tested while it is still on the wafer. Then the wafer is cut apart, and the good chips are packaged. Because chips are square and wafers are round, some silicon at the edge is always wasted. Try the calculator below to see how much.
paras_zh: 晶片的起點，是幾乎每個海灘都找得到的東西：沙子。大部分的沙子主要是石英，也就是矽和氧結合成的；矽是地殼裡第二多的元素。可是晶片需要的矽必須非常純、排列得非常整齊，所以把沙子變成晶片，是人類學過最講究的工作之一。
第一步，要把氧拿掉。工廠通常用高純度的石英岩，而不是沙灘的沙，把它和碳一起放進超過攝氏 2,000 度的電爐加熱。碳把氧帶走，留下純度約 98% 到 99% 的矽。聽起來很純，但對晶片來說還是太髒了。
接著用化學方法清潔矽。先把它變成一種叫「三氯矽烷」的液體，提純之後，再讓它在加熱到約 1,150 度的細矽棒上變回矽，矽棒慢慢長粗。這樣做出來的叫「多晶矽」，晶片用的純度至少是 99.99999999%，也就是一連十個 9。
多晶矽是由許多很小的晶體組成的，但晶片需要「一整塊」單晶。所以把矽加熱到 1,414 度熔化，把一小塊晶種浸進液體，一邊旋轉一邊慢慢往上拉。矽凝固在晶種上，每個原子都排成同一個方向，長成一根又長又亮的晶棒，可以長達約 2 公尺。這叫做「柴可拉斯基法」，名字來自 1916 年發明它的波蘭科學家。
然後，鋼線鋸把晶棒切成薄薄的圓片，叫做「晶圓」。晶圓經過研磨、蝕刻、拋光，亮得像鏡子一樣。今天先進晶片主要用的晶圓直徑 300 公釐，通常叫做 12 吋晶圓，厚度只有約 775 微米，不到 1 公釐。
最後，每片晶圓上一層一層、並排做出幾百顆晶片，下一課就會看到怎麼做。每顆晶片在還沒切開前就先在晶圓上測試，然後把晶圓切開，好的晶片拿去封裝。因為晶片是方的、晶圓是圓的，邊緣一定會浪費一些矽。用下面的計算器算算看浪費多少。

culture_cards.title_en: A pen, a reactor, a nickname, and Hsinchu
culture_cards.title_zh: 一支筆、一座反應爐、一個暱稱和新竹
culture_cards.lead_en: Four stories from the road between sand and chips.
culture_cards.lead_zh: 從沙子到晶片的路上，四個小故事。

cards.en: A pen in the wrong pot
cards.body_en: The story goes that in 1916, the Polish scientist Jan Czochralski dipped his pen into a pot of melted tin instead of his inkwell. When he pulled it out, a thin thread of tin came with it, and it was a single crystal. He reported his method in 1918, and today it is used to grow the silicon crystals for chips.
cards.body_zh: 相傳 1916 年，波蘭科學家柴可拉斯基把筆伸進一鍋熔化的錫，而不是墨水瓶。拿出來時，筆尖帶出一條細細的錫絲，竟然是一整塊單晶。他在 1918 年發表這個方法，今天晶片用的矽單晶就是這樣長出來的。

cards.body_en: In the 1950s, the German companies Siemens and Wacker developed a way to make ultra-pure silicon by growing it on hot, thin rods inside a bell-shaped reactor. It is still called the Siemens process, and for chips it reaches ten to eleven nines, from 99.99999999 to 99.999999999 percent pure.
cards.body_zh: 1950 年代，德國的西門子和瓦克公司發展出一種方法：在鐘形反應爐裡，讓矽長在發熱的細矽棒上，做出超高純度的矽。這方法至今仍叫「西門子法」，晶片用的純度達到十到十一個 9，也就是 99.99999999% 到 99.999999999%。

cards.body_en: A 300 mm wafer is really 11.8 inches across, but almost everyone calls it a 12-inch wafer, and a factory that uses it is a 12-inch fab, 12 吋晶圓廠 in Chinese. 300 mm wafers were introduced in 1999. A research group working on even bigger 450 mm wafers began shutting down in 2017.
cards.body_zh: 300 公釐的晶圓其實是 11.8 吋，但大家都叫它 12 吋晶圓，用它的工廠就叫「12 吋晶圓廠」。300 mm 晶圓在 1999 年推出；研究更大 450 mm 晶圓的聯盟，在 2017 年開始解散。

cards.k: Made in Taiwan · 台灣製造
cards.body_en: Taiwan also makes the blank silicon wafers that chips are built on. GlobalWafers, headquartered in Hsinchu Science Park, makes 300 mm and 200 mm wafers, and companies such as Wafer Works and Formosa SUMCO Technology also make silicon wafers in Taiwan.
cards.body_zh: 台灣也生產做晶片用的空白矽晶圓。總部在新竹科學園區的環球晶圓生產 12 吋和 8 吋晶圓；合晶科技、台塑勝高科技等公司也在台灣生產矽晶圓。

myths.myth_en: A silicon wafer is a kind of glass.
myths.myth_zh: 矽晶圓是一種玻璃。
myths.fact_en: Glass is amorphous: its atoms have no regular pattern. A wafer is a single crystal, with every atom lined up in the same pattern from edge to edge.
myths.fact_zh: 玻璃是非晶質，原子沒有規則的排列；晶圓是單晶，從這一邊到那一邊，每個原子都排成同一個圖樣。

myths.myth_en: Each chip is carved from its own little block of silicon.
myths.myth_zh: 每顆晶片都是從自己的一小塊矽雕出來的。
myths.fact_en: Hundreds of chips are made side by side on one wafer at the same time, then cut apart.
myths.fact_zh: 幾百顆晶片在同一片晶圓上同時並排做好，再切開。

myths.myth_en: Bigger wafers make bigger chips.
myths.myth_zh: 晶圓越大，晶片就越大。
myths.fact_en: A chip's size is set by its design. A bigger wafer simply fits more chips.
myths.fact_zh: 晶片的大小由設計決定；晶圓大，只是放得下更多晶片。

myths.myth_en: Every chip on a wafer works.
myths.myth_zh: 晶圓上每顆晶片都是好的。
myths.fact_en: Some don't. Every chip is tested while still on the wafer, and the bad ones are left out before packaging, which saves money.
myths.fact_zh: 有些是壞的。每顆晶片在晶圓上就先測試，壞的不拿去封裝，省下成本。

tricks.body_en: Five steps: quartz to silicon, purify it, grow one crystal, slice it into wafers.
tricks.body_zh: 石英變矽、提純、長成單晶、切成晶圓。

tricks.body_en: Every atom in the ingot lines up with the tiny seed it grew from.
tricks.body_zh: 晶棒裡每個原子，都跟著最上面那顆小晶種排隊。

tricks.body_en: Chips are made side by side on one wafer, then cut apart.
tricks.body_zh: 晶片在同一片晶圓上並排做好，再切開。

tricks.body_en: Squares never fill a circle; big chips leave more of the edge unused.
tricks.body_zh: 方格永遠填不滿圓，晶片越大，邊緣浪費越多。

safety.en: An adult must make and pour the hot sugar syrup. Boiling water and hot syrup can cause serious burns.
safety.zh: 熱糖漿一定要由大人煮、大人倒。滾水和熱糖漿會造成嚴重燙傷。

safety.en: Never try to melt sand, glass, or metal at home. The furnaces in this lesson are thousands of degrees and belong in factories.
safety.zh: 絕不要在家裡熔化沙子、玻璃或金屬。這一課的爐子有好幾千度，只能在工廠裡用。

safety.en: Be careful with the sharp point of a compass and with scissors.
safety.zh: 小心圓規的尖端和剪刀。

safety.en: Cover the crystal jar to keep out dust and insects, and throw it away if mold grows.
safety.zh: 養晶體的罐子要蓋好，防灰塵和昆蟲；如果發霉就丟掉。

activities.title_zh: 做一片真實大小的紙晶圓

materials.en: A large sheet of paper or cardboard, at least 32 cm wide
materials.zh: 一張至少 32 公分寬的大紙或紙板

materials.en: A compass, or a pin, string, and pencil
materials.zh: 圓規，或圖釘、細繩和鉛筆

materials.en: A ruler and colored pencils
materials.zh: 直尺和色鉛筆

steps.en: Draw a circle with a radius of 15 cm. It is exactly the size of a real 300 mm wafer.
steps.zh: 畫一個半徑 15 公分的圓，大小和真的 12 吋晶圓一模一樣。

steps.en: Draw a grid of 2 cm squares across the circle. Each square is a 20 mm chip.
steps.zh: 在圓上畫 2 公分的方格，每格是一顆 20 公釐的晶片。

steps.en: Color the squares that fit completely inside the circle, and count them. Shade the broken squares at the edge in gray.
steps.zh: 把完全在圓裡的方格塗色、數一數；邊緣不完整的方格塗灰色。

steps.en: Compare your count with the calculator for 20 mm chips. Then try 5 cm squares. Which size wastes more of the edge?
steps.zh: 和計算器 20 公釐的結果比一比；再試試 5 公分的方格。哪一種邊緣浪費比較多？

activities.tip_en: Your count may be a little higher than the calculator's, because the calculator keeps a 3 mm edge unused.
activities.tip_zh: 你數到的可能比計算器多一點，因為計算器留了 3 公釐的邊緣不用。

activities.title_en: Grow a Sugar Crystal from a Seed

materials.en: Sugar and water (about 2.5 cups of sugar for every cup of water)
materials.zh: 糖和水（大約每 1 杯水配 2.5 杯糖）

materials.en: A clean glass jar, a cotton string, and a pencil
materials.zh: 乾淨的玻璃罐、棉線和一支鉛筆

materials.en: A few grains of sugar to use as seeds
materials.zh: 幾粒當晶種用的砂糖

steps.en: Wet the string and roll it in sugar. These grains are your seed crystals.
steps.zh: 把棉線沾濕、在砂糖裡滾一滾，這些糖粒就是晶種。

steps.en: An adult heats the water, stirs in the sugar until it dissolves, and lets it cool a little before pouring it into the jar.
steps.zh: 請大人把水加熱，攪入糖直到溶化，稍微放涼後倒進罐子。

steps.en: Tie the string to the pencil and hang it in the syrup without touching the sides or bottom. Leave the jar still for several days.
steps.zh: 把棉線綁在鉛筆上，垂進糖漿裡，不要碰到罐子的側面和底部。靜置幾天。

steps.en: Look at the crystals with a magnifying glass. How did the seeds decide where the crystals grew? How is this like pulling a silicon crystal from a seed?
steps.zh: 用放大鏡看晶體：晶種怎麼決定晶體長在哪裡？這和用晶種拉出矽單晶有什麼像的地方？

activities.tip_en: Do not move or shake the jar while the crystals grow. This makes many small crystals, not a few big ones. Silicon crystals are pulled slowly and smoothly for the same reason.
activities.tip_zh: 晶體長大時不要移動或搖晃罐子，否則會長出很多小晶體，而不是幾塊大的。矽單晶要慢慢、平穩地拉，也是同樣的道理。

lessons.blurb_en: Chips are drawn with light. In 3D, watch light shine through a mask and shrink onto a wafer, switch from DUV to EUV light made by blasting drops of tin, then cut open the wafer to see the five steps that carve a pattern. Then make a sun print on your screen.
lessons.blurb_zh: 晶片是用光畫出來的。在 3D 裡看光穿過光罩、縮小印到晶圓上；從 DUV 切換到用雷射打錫滴產生的 EUV；再把晶圓剖開，看刻出圖案的五個步驟。最後在螢幕上曬一張藍曬圖。
lessons.big_idea_en: Chips are drawn with light. Light shines through a mask with the circuit pattern, lenses or mirrors shrink it onto a light-sensitive coating on the wafer, and the pattern is then etched in. This is repeated layer after layer, and the shorter the light's wavelength, the finer the lines.
lessons.big_idea_zh: 晶片是用光畫出來的：光穿過畫好電路的光罩，鏡頭或反射鏡把圖案縮小，印在晶圓的感光膠上，再把圖案蝕刻出來。一層一層重複做；光的波長越短，畫得越細。

lab.how_en: Drag to turn the model, and scroll or pinch to zoom. In The machine, watch the light print one field after another across the wafer, and switch between DUV and EUV light. Then choose On the wafer to see a slice of the wafer go through the five steps that carve the pattern.
lab.how_zh: 拖曳可以旋轉模型，滾輪或雙指可以縮放。在「曝光機」看光把晶圓一格一格印滿，並切換 DUV 和 EUV 兩種光；再選「晶圓上的步驟」，看晶圓剖面經過刻出圖案的五個步驟。

steps.text_en: The wafer already has a thin layer to be patterned. A light-sensitive coating called photoresist is spread over it, thin and even.
steps.text_zh: 晶圓上已經有一層要刻圖案的薄膜。先在上面塗一層又薄又均勻的感光膠，叫做「光阻」。

steps.text_en: Light passes through the clear parts of the mask and lands on the photoresist. The dark parts of the mask block it. Where light lands, the photoresist changes chemically.
steps.text_zh: 光穿過光罩透明的地方，照到光阻上；光罩上不透光的部分把光擋住。照到光的光阻，化學性質就改變了。

steps.text_en: A liquid called developer washes away the photoresist that was hit by light. This is how a positive photoresist works. Now the pattern is an open stencil.
steps.text_zh: 用顯影液把照過光的光阻洗掉（這是「正型光阻」的做法），光阻就變成一張開了洞的模板。

steps.text_en: Chemicals or a plasma eat away the layer wherever the photoresist is gone. Where photoresist remains, the layer is protected.
steps.text_zh: 用化學藥劑或電漿，把沒有光阻保護的薄膜蝕刻掉；還有光阻的地方，薄膜就被保護住。

steps.title_en: Remove the rest of the photoresist
steps.text_en: The leftover photoresist is removed, and the pattern from the mask is now carved into the layer. A chip repeats steps like these for layer after layer.
steps.text_zh: 把剩下的光阻去掉，光罩上的圖案就刻進薄膜裡了。一顆晶片要這樣一層又一層地重複做。

m_duv.en: Deep ultraviolet (DUV) light from a laser shines through the mask, and a stack of glass lenses shrinks the pattern four times onto one field of the wafer. Then the wafer moves, and the next field is printed.
m_duv.zh: 雷射發出的深紫外光（DUV）穿過光罩，一疊玻璃鏡頭把圖案縮小 4 倍，印在晶圓的一格上；接著晶圓移動，再印下一格。

m_euv.en: Extreme ultraviolet (EUV) light has a much shorter wavelength, so it can print finer lines. But glass and even air absorb it, so the machine uses mirrors instead of lenses and works in a vacuum. The light is made by a laser hitting tiny drops of tin.
m_euv.zh: 極紫外光（EUV）的波長短得多，可以印出更細的線。但玻璃、甚至空氣都會吸收它，所以機器改用反射鏡、在真空中工作。這種光是雷射打在小錫滴上產生的。

w.en: This is a tiny slice of the wafer, cut open. Press the steps, or play all five, to see how the pattern on the mask ends up carved into the layer. Switch between DUV and EUV to compare how fine the lines are.
w.zh: 這是晶圓上一小塊的剖面。按每一步，或連續播放五步，看光罩上的圖案怎麼刻進薄膜裡。切換 DUV 和 EUV，比比看線條有多細。

legend.zh: 紫色光束：紫外光（真實是看不見的）

legend.en: Orange: photoresist, the light-sensitive coating
legend.zh: 橘色：光阻，會感光的膜

legend.en: Blue: the layer being patterned
legend.zh: 藍色：要刻出圖案的薄膜

legend.en: Silver: mirrors, chrome on the mask, the silicon wafer
legend.zh: 銀色：反射鏡、光罩上的鉻、矽晶圓

lab.scale_en: A teaching diagram, not to scale. Ultraviolet light is invisible; it is drawn purple. A real machine is about the size of a bus, with many more mirrors and lenses than shown. In the wafer slice, the number of lines follows the finest line each light can print (about 57 nm for DUV and 16 nm for EUV), but the drawing is enlarged millions of times.
lab.scale_zh: 這是示意圖，不是真實比例。紫外光其實看不見，這裡畫成紫色。真的機器大約有一台公車那麼大，反射鏡和鏡頭也比圖上多得多。晶圓剖面裡的線條數，是照兩種光能印出的最細線寬（DUV 約 57 奈米、EUV 約 16 奈米）的比例畫的，但整張圖放大了好幾百萬倍。

paras: A transistor in a modern chip is far too small to draw with a pen, a laser, or even the sharpest needle. A flu virus is only about 80 to 120 nanometers across, and many lines in a chip are thinner than that. So how do engineers draw billions of them at once? They use light as a pen. The process is called photolithography, from Greek words meaning writing on stone with light.

It works a bit like a stencil. First, the wafer is coated with photoresist, a thin film that changes when light hits it. The circuit pattern is drawn on a mask, a plate of quartz glass with chrome where light should be blocked. Light shines through the mask, and lenses shrink the pattern four times before it lands on the wafer.

Next, the wafer is washed in a liquid called developer. In the most common kind of photoresist, the parts hit by light wash away, so the photoresist becomes a stencil with tiny openings. Chemicals or a plasma etch the layer underneath through the openings, and then the leftover photoresist is removed. The pattern from the mask is now carved into the chip.

One pattern is not enough. A chip is built up layer by layer: transistors at the bottom, then many layers of tiny metal wires above them. ASML, the Dutch company that makes the most advanced lithography machines, says a modern chip can need up to about 100 patterning steps. Every layer has to line up with the one below it almost perfectly.

Why use such special light? The finest line light can draw depends on its wavelength. Many machines use deep ultraviolet (DUV) light with a wavelength of 193 nanometers. The newest use extreme ultraviolet (EUV) light at just 13.5 nanometers, more than 14 times shorter. EUV light is made by hitting tiny drops of tin with lasers, 50,000 drops every second. Even air absorbs it, so an EUV machine works in a vacuum and uses mirrors instead of lenses.

A single speck of dust could ruin a pattern this small, so chips are made in cleanrooms. In the cleanest kind, ISO class 1, a cubic meter of air may hold no more than 10 particles bigger than 0.1 micrometers. Ordinary room air is around class 9, and each step up the scale allows about ten times more particles. The rooms where photoresist is handled are lit with yellow light, because blue and ultraviolet light would expose it by accident.
paras_zh: 現代晶片裡的電晶體，小到用筆、用雷射、甚至最尖的針都畫不出來。一個流感病毒只有約 80 到 120 奈米寬，而晶片裡很多線條比這還細。工程師怎麼一次畫出幾十億個？他們用光當筆。這個過程叫做「微影」（photolithography），英文字源於希臘文，意思是「用光在石頭上寫字」。
它有點像用模板噴畫。首先，在晶圓上塗一層光阻：照到光就會改變的薄膜。電路圖案畫在「光罩」上，那是一片石英玻璃，要擋光的地方鍍上鉻。光穿過光罩，鏡頭把圖案縮小 4 倍，再落到晶圓上。
接著，用一種叫「顯影液」的液體沖洗晶圓。最常見的光阻，照到光的部分會被洗掉，光阻就變成一張有細小開口的模板。再用化學藥劑或電漿，從開口把底下那層蝕刻掉，最後去掉剩下的光阻。光罩上的圖案就刻進晶片裡了。
一次圖案是不夠的。晶片是一層一層蓋起來的：最下面是電晶體，上面是好多層極細的金屬導線。製造最先進曝光機的荷蘭公司艾司摩爾（ASML）說，一顆現代晶片最多需要約 100 次圖案步驟。每一層都必須和下面那一層幾乎完美地對齊。
為什麼要用這麼特別的光？光能畫出多細的線，取決於它的波長。很多機器用波長 193 奈米的深紫外光（DUV）；最新的機器用只有 13.5 奈米的極紫外光（EUV），短了 14 倍以上。EUV 是用雷射打在小小的錫滴上產生的，每秒 5 萬滴。連空氣都會吸收它，所以 EUV 機器要在真空中工作，並且用反射鏡代替鏡頭。
一粒灰塵就能毀掉這麼小的圖案，所以晶片要在無塵室裡做。最乾淨的 ISO 1 級無塵室，每立方公尺空氣裡大於 0.1 微米的微粒不能超過 10 顆。一般室內空氣大約是 9 級，而等級每往上一級，允許的微粒大約多 10 倍。處理光阻的房間用黃色的燈光，因為藍光和紫外光會不小心讓光阻感光。
questions: What does the mask do?
What happens to the most common kind of photoresist where light hits it?
Why does an EUV machine use mirrors and work in a vacuum?
answers: It carries the circuit pattern. Light passes through its clear parts and is blocked by the chrome.
Those parts wash away in the developer, leaving a stencil with tiny openings.
Glass and even air absorb EUV light, so it must travel in a vacuum and bounce off mirrors.

parts.text_en: Light from a laser passes through the mask and a stack of lenses, and prints one field after another across the wafer.
parts.text_zh: 雷射光穿過光罩和一疊鏡頭，把晶圓一格一格印滿。

parts.text_en: Laser pulses flash tin drops into glowing plasma, and the light bounces off mirrors and a reflective mask.
parts.text_zh: 雷射把錫滴打成發光的電漿，光經過反射鏡和反射式光罩一路彈到晶圓上。

parts.text_en: Watch a slice of the wafer as the mask's pattern is carved into the layer.

parts.meta_zh: 約 57 奈米對 16 奈米
parts.text_en: Switch the light and compare the finished lines: EUV's are about three and a half times finer.
parts.text_zh: 切換光源，比較刻好的線：EUV 的線大約細了三倍半。

lessons.parts_note_en: ASML gives the finest line as about k1 × wavelength ÷ NA. NA describes how widely the lenses or mirrors gather light, and k1 is usually about 0.4. EUV's wavelength is 14 times shorter, but its mirrors gather light less widely, so its lines are about 3.5 times finer, not 14.
lessons.parts_note_zh: ASML 說，最細的線約等於 k1 × 波長 ÷ NA。NA 表示鏡頭或反射鏡收光的範圍有多大，k1 通常約 0.4。EUV 的波長短了 14 倍，但它的反射鏡收光範圍比較小，所以線條細了約 3.5 倍，而不是 14 倍。

sunprint.eyebrow: Make a Sun Print · 曬一張藍曬圖
sunprint.en: Print with light on your screen
sunprint.lead_en: This is how blueprints were made, and it works like a lithography machine without the lens. Choose a mask, leave the paper in the sun, then wash it. Try lifting the mask away from the paper.
sunprint.lead_zh: 藍圖（blueprint）就是這樣做的，原理像少了鏡頭的曝光機。選一張光罩，讓紙曬太陽，再用水沖洗。試試看把光罩拿離紙面。
sunprint.note_en: The times are only examples. Real cyanotype paper needs anywhere from a few minutes to about 40 minutes, depending on the sun and the paper. The blur shows why a lithography machine must focus light so precisely: when shadows are fuzzy, thin lines run together.
sunprint.note_zh: 時間只是示例：真的藍曬紙要曬幾分鐘到大約 40 分鐘，看陽光和紙而定。模糊的效果說明了曝光機為什麼要把光聚得那麼準：影子一糊，細線就連在一起了。

culture_cards.title_en: A word, a blueprint, a giant machine, and yellow light
culture_cards.title_zh: 一個詞、一張藍圖、一台巨大的機器、一種黃色的光
culture_cards.lead_en: Four stories about drawing with light.
culture_cards.lead_zh: 關於「用光畫畫」的四個小故事。

cards.body_en: In 1957, Jay Lathrop and James Nall, working for the U.S. Army, patented a way to use light-sensitive coatings to pattern tiny metal strips for transistors. The word photolithography first appeared in print for this work in 1958. It comes from Greek: photo means light, litho means stone, and graphy means writing.
cards.body_zh: 1957 年，替美國陸軍工作的拉斯羅普和納爾，取得一項專利：用感光塗料替電晶體做出細小的金屬條。1958 年，photolithography（微影）這個詞第一次為這項技術出現在刊物上。它來自希臘文：photo 是光、litho 是石頭、graphy 是書寫。

cards.body_en: In 1842, the British scientist John Herschel published the cyanotype, a process that turns paper blue where light hits it. In 1843, Anna Atkins used it to make Photographs of British Algae, often called the first book illustrated with photographs. Architects and engineers later copied drawings this way, which is why we still say blueprint.
cards.body_zh: 1842 年，英國科學家赫歇爾發表了「氰版照相」（藍曬）：紙張照到光的地方會變藍。1843 年，安娜．阿特金斯用它做出《英國藻類照片集》，常被稱為第一本用照片做插圖的書。後來建築師和工程師用這種方法複製圖紙，所以我們今天還說「藍圖」。

cards.en: A machine the size of a bus
cards.body_en: As of 2025, ASML, based in Veldhoven in the Netherlands, is the only company that makes EUV machines for chip production. Reuters describes one as about the size of a school bus and weighing about 150 tons, shipped in around 40 containers.
cards.body_zh: 到 2025 年為止，總部在荷蘭費爾德霍溫的艾司摩爾（ASML），是世界上唯一生產晶片用 EUV 曝光機的公司。路透社形容一台大約像一輛校車那麼大、重約 150 公噸，要裝約 40 個貨櫃運送。

cards.zh: 微影區為什麼是黃色的
cards.body_en: Photoresist reacts to blue and ultraviolet light, so the parts of a cleanroom where it is used are lit with yellow light that leaves it alone. One photoresist maker says light shorter than 500 nanometers must be filtered out.
cards.body_zh: 光阻會對藍光和紫外光起反應，所以無塵室裡使用光阻的區域，都用不會讓它感光的黃色燈光。一家光阻廠商說，波長短於 500 奈米的光都要濾掉。

myths.myth_en: Chips are drawn line by line by a tiny robot pen or laser.
myths.myth_zh: 晶片是用很小的機器筆或雷射一條一條畫出來的。
myths.fact_en: A whole field of the pattern is printed at once with light through a mask, a bit like taking a photograph.
myths.fact_zh: 光穿過光罩，一次就印出一整格的圖案，有點像拍照。

myths.myth_en: EUV light is just very bright purple light.
myths.myth_zh: EUV 就是很亮的紫色光。
myths.fact_en: EUV light is invisible, with a wavelength far shorter than any color we can see. Even air absorbs it.
myths.fact_zh: EUV 是看不見的光，波長比任何看得見的顏色都短得多，連空氣都會吸收它。

myths.myth_en: The mask is the same size as the chip.
myths.myth_zh: 光罩和晶片一樣大。
myths.fact_en: The pattern on the mask is four times larger. The machine's optics shrink it onto the wafer.
myths.fact_zh: 光罩上的圖案是 4 倍大，由機器的光學系統縮小印到晶圓上。

myths.myth_en: One trip through the machine makes a chip.
myths.myth_zh: 晶片進曝光機一次就做好了。
myths.fact_en: A modern chip can need up to about 100 patterning steps, one layer on top of another.
myths.fact_zh: 一顆現代晶片最多約要 100 次圖案步驟，一層疊一層。

tricks.body_en: Five steps carve one pattern into one layer.
tricks.body_zh: 五個步驟，把一個圖案刻進一層。

tricks.body_en: The pattern shrinks four times on the way to the wafer.
tricks.body_zh: 圖案到晶圓上縮小 4 倍。

tricks.body_en: 193 nm DUV, 13.5 nm EUV.
tricks.body_zh: DUV 193 奈米，EUV 13.5 奈米。

tricks.body_en: Glass and air absorb it, so no lenses and no air.
tricks.body_zh: 玻璃和空氣都會吸收它，所以不用鏡頭、不要空氣。

safety.en: Never look directly at the sun, even through sunglasses or colored plastic.
safety.zh: 絕不要直視太陽，戴太陽眼鏡或透過有色塑膠片也不行。

safety.en: Use ready-made sun-print paper. If older students mix cyanotype chemicals, an adult must supervise; wear gloves and goggles, and keep the chemicals away from strong acids.
safety.zh: 請用現成的藍曬紙。如果高年級學生要自己調藍曬藥劑，一定要有大人在旁，戴手套和護目鏡，並且遠離強酸。

safety.en: Wash your hands after handling sun-print paper.
safety.zh: 碰過藍曬紙之後要洗手。

safety.en: Use a flashlight, not a laser pointer, and never shine light into anyone's eyes.
safety.zh: 用手電筒，不要用雷射筆；也絕不要把光照向別人的眼睛。

safety.en: An adult should handle the glass from a picture frame, or use a clear plastic sheet instead.
safety.zh: 相框的玻璃請大人拿；也可以改用透明塑膠片。

materials.en: Sun-print (cyanotype) paper from a craft or science shop
materials.zh: 美術或科學用品店買的藍曬紙

materials.en: Flat objects such as leaves and paper clips, or a stencil cut from cardboard
materials.zh: 葉子、迴紋針這類扁平的東西，或用紙板剪的模板

materials.en: A clear plastic sheet, and a tray of water
materials.zh: 一張透明塑膠片，和一盤清水

steps.en: Indoors, away from bright light, lay the paper blue side up and arrange your objects on it.
steps.zh: 在室內、避開強光，把藍曬紙藍色那面朝上，擺上你的東西。

steps.en: Cover them with the clear sheet so they stay flat, then carry everything into the sun.
steps.zh: 蓋上透明塑膠片把東西壓平，再拿到太陽下。

steps.en: Wait until the paper turns pale, following the time on the package. Then rinse it in water and let it dry.
steps.zh: 照包裝上的時間，等紙變淡，再放進水裡沖洗、晾乾。

steps.en: Compare the edges. Which objects gave sharp edges, and which gave blurry ones? How is this like a lithography machine?
steps.zh: 比較邊緣：哪些東西印出的邊很清楚、哪些比較模糊？這和曝光機有什麼像的地方？

activities.tip_en: Try one object lifted a few centimeters above the paper. Its print will be fuzzier, just like an image that is out of focus.
activities.tip_zh: 試試看把一樣東西架高幾公分，它印出來會比較模糊，就像沒對準焦的影像。

activities.title_en: Shrink a Pattern with a Lens

materials.en: A flashlight and a magnifying glass
materials.zh: 一支手電筒和一個放大鏡

materials.en: A clear plastic sheet with a simple pattern drawn in black marker
materials.zh: 一張用黑色麥克筆畫了簡單圖案的透明片

materials.en: A sheet of white paper as a screen, in a dim room
materials.zh: 一張白紙當屏幕，在昏暗的房間裡

steps.en: Hold the drawn sheet in front of the flashlight so light passes through the pattern.
steps.zh: 把畫了圖案的透明片放在手電筒前面，讓光穿過圖案。

steps.en: Hold the magnifying glass between the pattern and the white paper.
steps.zh: 把放大鏡放在圖案和白紙之間。

steps.en: Slowly move the paper and the lens until a sharp image of the pattern appears. Can you make it smaller than the drawing?
steps.zh: 慢慢移動白紙和放大鏡，直到出現清楚的圖案影像。你能讓它比原圖還小嗎？

steps.en: Notice that the image is upside down. Talk about it: a lithography machine shrinks its mask pattern four times in the same way, but with many lenses or mirrors.
steps.zh: 注意影像是上下顛倒的。討論：曝光機也是這樣把光罩圖案縮小 4 倍，只是用了很多鏡頭或反射鏡。

activities.tip_en: If the image is blurry, move the paper a little closer to or farther from the lens. Finding the sharpest spot is called focusing.
activities.tip_zh: 影像模糊時，把紙稍微移近或移遠一點；找到最清楚的位置，就叫做對焦。

sources.en: KrF 248 nm and ArF 193 nm lasers; EUV 13.5 nm, more than 14 times shorter; tin droplets 50,000 times a second, hit by two laser pulses
sources.zh: KrF 248、ArF 193 奈米雷射；EUV 13.5 奈米，短 14 倍以上；錫滴每秒 5 萬次、每滴兩道雷射脈衝

sources.en: EUV light is absorbed by everything, even air; high vacuum and multilayer mirrors; NA 0.33 and 0.55
sources.zh: EUV 光什麼都會吸收、連空氣也是；高真空與多層膜反射鏡；NA 0.33 與 0.55

sources.en: The blueprint (mask) is four times larger than the pattern on the chip; the process is repeated about 100 times
sources.zh: 光罩圖案是晶片上的 4 倍；這個過程重複約 100 次

sources.en: Resolution: CD = k1 × λ / NA; k1's physical limit is 0.25
sources.zh: 解析度：CD ＝ k1 × λ ／ NA；k1 物理極限 0.25

sources.en: Photolithography steps; positive photoresist is the most common; k1 about 0.4 in production; immersion with water
sources.zh: 微影步驟；正型光阻最常見；量產 k1 約 0.4；浸潤式用水

sources.en: Positive photoresist: exposed parts become soluble in developer
sources.zh: 正型光阻：照光的部分會溶於顯影液

sources.en: Immersion lithography: example of a 1.35 NA tool at 193 nm
sources.zh: 浸潤式微影：193 奈米、NA 1.35 的例子

sources.en: EUV light is absorbed by glass and air; field size 26 × 33 mm; ASML the only producer of EUV systems as of 2025
sources.zh: EUV 會被玻璃和空氣吸收；曝光範圍 26 × 33 mm；到 2025 年 ASML 是唯一的 EUV 製造商

sources.en: Photomask: quartz (fused silica) plate with a chromium pattern; shrunk four or five times
sources.zh: 光罩：石英玻璃上鍍鉻的圖案；縮小 4 或 5 倍

sources.en: ASML's global headquarters is in Veldhoven, the Netherlands
sources.zh: ASML 全球總部在荷蘭費爾德霍溫

sources.en: An EUV machine: about the size of a school bus, about 150 tons, shipped in around 40 containers (2026)
sources.zh: EUV 機台：約一輛校車大、約 150 公噸、約 40 個貨櫃運送（2026）

sources.en: Cleanroom classes (ISO 14644-1): ISO 1 allows 10 particles ≥0.1 µm per m³; ordinary room air is around ISO 9; yellow lighting for photolithography
sources.zh: 無塵室等級（ISO 14644-1）：ISO 1 每立方公尺 0.1 µm 以上微粒 10 顆；一般室內約 ISO 9；微影區用黃光

sources.en: Yellow light: wavelengths below 500 nm must be blocked for photoresist
sources.zh: 黃光：光阻區要擋掉 500 奈米以下的光

sources.en: Influenza A virions are 80–120 nm in diameter
sources.zh: A 型流感病毒直徑 80–120 奈米

sources.en: Lathrop and Nall patented photolithographic techniques in 1957
sources.zh: 拉斯羅普與納爾 1957 年取得微影技術專利

sources.en: Cyanotype: published by Herschel in 1842; ferric ammonium citrate and potassium ferricyanide; blueprints
sources.zh: 藍曬：赫歇爾 1842 年發表；檸檬酸鐵銨與鐵氰化鉀；藍圖

sources.en: Anna Atkins' 1843 book of cyanotypes; exposure 10–40 minutes; fixed by washing in water
sources.zh: 安娜．阿特金斯 1843 年的藍曬書；曝光 10–40 分鐘；用水沖洗定影

sources.en: Cyanotype safety for schools: gloves, goggles, hand washing, keep away from strong acids (2025)
sources.zh: 學校藍曬安全：手套、護目鏡、洗手、遠離強酸（2025）

lessons.title: How Small Is a Nanometer? An Angstrom?
lessons.blurb_en: News about chips is full of nanometers and angstroms. Zoom in 3D from your fingernail to a hair, a blood cell, a virus, the lines on a chip, and at last single silicon atoms. Then find out how many nanometers your nails have grown since you opened this page.
lessons.blurb_zh: 晶片的新聞裡到處是奈米和埃米。在 3D 裡從指甲一路放大：頭髮、紅血球、病毒、晶片上的線，最後是一顆顆矽原子。再算算看，從你打開這一頁到現在，指甲長了幾奈米。
lessons.big_idea_en: A nanometer is one billionth of a meter, and an angstrom is one tenth of a nanometer, about the size of a single atom. The lines on today's chips are tens of nanometers apart. Names like “3 nanometer” and “2 nanometer” are names for generations of chips, not lengths that anyone measured.
lessons.big_idea_zh: 1 奈米是十億分之一公尺；1 埃米是十分之一奈米，差不多就是一顆原子的大小。現在晶片上的線，彼此相隔幾十奈米。「3 奈米」「2 奈米」是每一代晶片的名字，不是量出來的長度。

lab.title_en: Zoom In, Ten Times at a Time
lab.how_en: Drag the Zoom slider, press × 10, or pick one of the eight stops. The yellow bracket at the bottom is a ruler: its length is written beside it, and it changes as you zoom. Watch the units change from centimeters to millimeters, micrometers, nanometers, and finally angstroms. You can also drag the picture to turn it.
lab.how_zh: 拉「縮放」滑桿、按「× 10」，或直接選八站裡的一站。下方黃色的括號是一把尺：旁邊寫著它有多長，放大的時候會跟著換。注意單位怎麼從公分變成公釐、微米、奈米，最後變成埃米。也可以拖曳畫面轉一轉。

stops.text_en: Start with something you can see. A fingernail is about 1 centimeter wide, which is 10 million nanometers.
stops.text_zh: 從看得到的東西開始。指甲大約 1 公分寬，也就是 1,000 萬奈米。

stops.text_en: Human hairs are between 17 and 181 micrometers thick; 75 is a common round number. A micrometer is one thousandth of a millimeter.
stops.text_zh: 人的頭髮粗細在 17 到 181 微米之間，常取 75 微米當代表。1 微米是千分之一公釐。

stops.title_en: A red blood cell: about 7 micrometers
stops.text_en: A red blood cell is a disk about 6 to 8 micrometers across. Ten of them side by side are as wide as one hair.
stops.text_zh: 紅血球是直徑大約 6 到 8 微米的圓盤。十個排成一排，差不多是一根頭髮寬。

stops.text_en: An E. coli bacterium is a rod about 2 micrometers long. This is close to the smallest thing an ordinary light microscope shows well.
stops.text_zh: 一隻大腸桿菌是長約 2 微米的小桿子。這已經接近一般光學顯微鏡看得清楚的最小東西。

stops.title_zh: 流感病毒：大約 100 奈米
stops.text_en: Now we are counting in nanometers. A flu virus is 80 to 120 nanometers across, too small for a light microscope to show clearly.
stops.text_zh: 現在開始用奈米來算了。流感病毒的直徑是 80 到 120 奈米，小到光學顯微鏡看不清楚。

stops.title_en: Lines on a chip: 24 nanometers apart
stops.title_zh: 晶片上的線：相隔 24 奈米
stops.text_en: In a chip called “3 nanometer,” the closest metal lines are expected to be 24 nanometers apart. The little yellow bar shows how short 3 nanometers really is.
stops.text_zh: 在一顆叫做「3 奈米」的晶片裡，最密的金屬線預計相隔 24 奈米。那條黃色的小橫槓，就是 3 奈米真正的長度。

stops.text_en: The twisted ladder of DNA is about 2 nanometers wide. Scientists often write that as 20 angstroms.
stops.text_zh: DNA 這條扭轉的梯子大約 2 奈米寬，科學家常把它寫成 20 埃米。

stops.text_en: At last, single atoms. Neighboring silicon atoms sit about 0.24 nanometers apart, or 2.4 angstroms. The yellow bar is 1 angstrom long.
stops.text_zh: 終於看到一顆顆原子了。相鄰的矽原子相隔大約 0.24 奈米，也就是 2.4 埃米。黃色的橫槓長 1 埃米。

legend.en: Yellow bracket: the ruler for the picture you are looking at
legend.zh: 黃色括號：目前這個畫面的比例尺

legend.en: Yellow bars in the model: 3 nanometers (at the chip lines) and 1 angstrom (at the atoms)
legend.zh: 模型裡的黃色橫槓：3 奈米（在晶片的線那一站）和 1 埃米（在原子那一站）

legend.en: The floor takes the color of the thing you have zoomed into
legend.zh: 地板的顏色，就是你鑽進去的那個東西的顏色

lab.scale_en: Every object is drawn at its true size compared with the others, so this model is to scale. The shapes are simplified, and the objects are simply stacked on one another so that you can compare them: a virus does not really sit on a bacterium, and chips are not made on DNA. The fingernail's width (about 1 centimeter) is a round number. Real atoms are not hard balls.
lab.scale_zh: 每一樣東西都照彼此的真實大小比例畫，所以這個模型是「照比例」的。形狀是簡化的，而且只是把它們一個疊在一個上面方便比較：病毒並不是真的坐在細菌上，晶片也不是做在 DNA 上。指甲的寬度（約 1 公分）是取整數。真正的原子也不是硬硬的小球。
lab.credit_html: Model drawn by My Culture Connect as a teaching diagram. The sizes come from the sources listed at the bottom of this page; the chip line spacing is the IRDS 2021 figure quoted in Wikipedia, “3 nm process”. · 模型由人師教育協會自繪示意；各項大小依本頁最下方列出的出處，晶片線距採用維基百科「3 nm process」條目引用的 IRDS 2021 數字。

paras: Turn on the news in Taiwan and you will hear about 3-nanometer chips, 2-nanometer chips, and now chips measured in angstroms. These words sound very small, and they are. But how small? Smaller than a hair? Smaller than a germ? Let us take a trip down to the bottom, ten times smaller at each step.

Start with your fingernail, about one centimeter wide. Zoom in about a hundred times and you reach a single hair, about 75 micrometers thick. A micrometer is one thousandth of a millimeter. Zoom in ten times more and you meet a red blood cell, about 7 micrometers across. A bacterium is smaller still, about 2 micrometers long.

Keep going, and micrometers become too big. We need a smaller unit: the nanometer, one thousandth of a micrometer, or one billionth of a meter. A flu virus is about 100 nanometers across. The finest lines on a modern chip are a few tens of nanometers apart. A strand of DNA is only about 2 nanometers wide.

At the very bottom are atoms. Silicon atoms in a chip sit about 0.24 nanometers from their neighbors. For sizes like this, scientists use an even smaller unit, the angstrom, which is one tenth of a nanometer. It is named after Anders Ångström, a Swedish scientist. So one silicon atom is a little more than 2 angstroms wide.

Now for a surprise. A “3-nanometer chip” does not have parts that are 3 nanometers wide. Long ago, the number in the name was a real length on the chip. Today it is only a name for a generation of chips: a smaller number means a newer design that packs in more transistors. In a “3-nanometer” chip, the closest metal lines are expected to be about 24 nanometers apart.

Names with angstroms work the same way. One chip maker uses names like 18A, and another uses A16, where the A stands for angstrom. They tell you which generation a chip belongs to, not what a ruler would read. Still, the real sizes are amazing. Chip makers now build parts only a few dozen atoms wide, billions of times on every chip.
paras_zh: 在台灣打開新聞，常會聽到 3 奈米晶片、2 奈米晶片，現在還有用「埃米」來算的晶片。這些詞聽起來很小，也真的很小。可是到底多小？比頭髮細嗎？比細菌小嗎？我們一路往下走，每一步都縮小十倍。
從你的指甲開始，寬度大約 1 公分。放大大約一百倍，會看到一根頭髮，粗細大約 75 微米。1 微米是千分之一公釐。再放大十倍，會遇到紅血球，直徑大約 7 微米。細菌又更小，大約 2 微米長。
繼續往下，微米就太大了，我們需要更小的單位：奈米。1 奈米是千分之一微米，也就是十億分之一公尺。流感病毒的直徑大約 100 奈米。現代晶片上最細的線，彼此相隔幾十奈米。一條 DNA 只有大約 2 奈米寬。
最底下是原子。晶片裡的矽原子，和旁邊的原子相隔大約 0.24 奈米。這麼小的尺寸，科學家用一個更小的單位，叫做埃米（也寫成「埃」），是十分之一奈米。它是用瑞典科學家埃格斯特朗（Anders Ångström）的名字命名的。所以一顆矽原子的寬度是 2 埃米多一點。
接下來的事可能讓你很意外：「3 奈米晶片」裡面，並沒有哪個零件是 3 奈米寬。很久以前，名字裡的數字確實是晶片上量得到的長度。現在它只是一代晶片的名字：數字越小，代表設計越新、塞進去的電晶體越多。在一顆「3 奈米」的晶片裡，最密的金屬線預計相隔大約 24 奈米。
用埃米取的名字也是一樣。有一家晶片公司用 18A 這樣的名字，另一家用 A16，其中的 A 就是埃米（angstrom）。這些名字告訴你晶片屬於哪一代，不是用尺量出來的讀數。不過真正的尺寸還是很驚人：晶片公司現在做出來的零件只有幾十顆原子寬，而且每一顆晶片上要做幾十億次。
questions: How big is a nanometer, and how big is an angstrom?
Which is smaller: a flu virus or the spacing between the finest lines on a modern chip?
What does the “3” in “3-nanometer chip” tell you?
answers: A nanometer is one billionth of a meter. An angstrom is one tenth of a nanometer, about the size of a single atom.
The spacing between the lines on the chip. It is a few tens of nanometers, and a flu virus is about 100 nanometers across.
It is the name of a generation of chips. A smaller number means a newer design with more transistors. It is not a length that anyone measured on the chip.

parts.text_en: The last thing on this trip that your eyes can see without help. Everything after this needs a microscope.
parts.text_zh: 這趟旅程裡，眼睛不靠工具還看得到的最後一樣東西。再往下都需要顯微鏡。

parts.text_en: Here the unit changes from micrometers to nanometers. Look how small the virus is beside the bacterium.
parts.text_zh: 單位從微米換成奈米了。看看病毒在細菌旁邊有多小。

parts.text_en: Find the little yellow bar. That is 3 nanometers. The lines of a “3-nanometer” chip are much farther apart than that.
parts.text_zh: 找找那條黃色的小橫槓，那就是 3 奈米。「3 奈米」晶片上的線，間距比它大得多。

parts.text_en: The bottom of the trip. From your fingernail to here, the picture has been magnified more than 40 million times.

lessons.parts_note_zh: 每按一次「× 10」，畫面就窄十倍。從指甲到原子，大約要按七次。

nail.eyebrow: Your Own Nanometers · 你自己的奈米
nail.en: How much have your nails grown?
nail.lead_en: Fingernails grow about 3.5 millimeters a month. That sounds slow, but in nanometers it is more than one every second. The counter started when you opened this page.
nail.lead_zh: 指甲平均每個月大約長 3.5 公釐。聽起來很慢，但換成奈米，每秒就長一奈米多。右邊的數字從你打開這一頁就開始算了。
nail.note_en: The growth rate is an average for healthy young adults; your own nails may be faster or slower. The paper is cut along its long side, 297 millimeters. Real scissors give up after six or seven cuts, but the arithmetic keeps going.
nail.note_zh: 生長速度是健康年輕人的平均值，你自己的指甲可能快一點或慢一點。紙是沿著長邊（297 公釐）剪的；真的剪刀剪六、七次就剪不下去了，但算術可以一直算下去。

facts.eyebrow: Small by the Numbers · 小的數字
facts.en: From a billionth of a meter to an atom
facts.zh: 從十億分之一公尺到一顆原子
facts.lead_zh: 六個幫你想像「小」的數字。

items.en: A nanometer is 0.000000001 meter. A billion of them in a row make one meter.
items.zh: 1 奈米是 0.000000001 公尺。十億個排成一排才是 1 公尺。

items.en: An angstrom is about the size of one atom. Ten angstroms make one nanometer.
items.zh: 1 埃米差不多是一顆原子的大小。10 埃米是 1 奈米。

items.en: Neighboring silicon atoms in a crystal are about this far apart: 2.4 angstroms.
items.zh: 晶體裡相鄰的矽原子大約相隔這麼遠，也就是 2.4 埃米。

items.en: The expected spacing of the closest metal lines in a “3-nanometer” chip, eight times the number in its name.
items.zh: 「3 奈米」晶片裡最密的金屬線預計的間距，是名字裡那個數字的八倍。

items.en: At 3.5 millimeters a month, a fingernail grows about this much every second.
items.zh: 每個月長 3.5 公釐的指甲，每秒大約長這麼多。

items.en: Cut a strip of A4 paper in half this many times and it would be less than 1 nanometer long.
items.zh: 把一條 A4 紙對半剪這麼多次，它的長度就不到 1 奈米了。

culture_cards.eyebrow: Stories of Small Units · 小單位的故事
culture_cards.title_en: A dwarf, a Swedish scientist, a name, and a letter A
culture_cards.title_zh: 一個小矮人、一位瑞典科學家、一個名字、一個字母 A
culture_cards.lead_en: Four stories behind the words in the news.
culture_cards.lead_zh: 新聞裡那些詞背後的四個小故事。

cards.body_en: The prefix nano comes from the Greek word nanos, which means dwarf. In 1960 it was officially approved as the prefix for one billionth. In Taiwan it is written 奈米; you may also see 納米 in other places.
cards.body_zh: 字首 nano 來自希臘文的 nanos，意思是「矮人」。1960 年，它正式成為代表「十億分之一」的字首。台灣寫成「奈米」，在其他地方也會看到「納米」。

cards.body_en: In 1868 the Swedish physicist Anders Ångström made a chart of the colors in sunlight. He wrote the wavelengths in units of one ten-millionth of a millimeter. That unit was later named the angstrom after him. It is not an official SI unit, but scientists still use it for atoms.
cards.body_zh: 1868 年，瑞典物理學家埃格斯特朗把陽光裡的各種顏色畫成一張圖表，波長用「千萬分之一公釐」當單位。這個單位後來就用他的名字命名為埃米。它不是國際單位制（SI）的正式單位，但科學家講原子時還是常用。

cards.body_en: An international roadmap for the chip industry says that a “3-nanometer” chip is expected to have gates 48 nanometers apart and metal lines 24 nanometers apart. Nothing in it is 3 nanometers. The number is a label that tells you the generation.
cards.body_zh: 半導體產業的一份國際技術藍圖指出，「3 奈米」晶片的閘極預計相隔 48 奈米、金屬線相隔 24 奈米，裡面沒有任何東西是 3 奈米。這個數字是一個標籤，告訴你它是哪一代。

cards.body_en: In 2021 Intel began naming its newest generations with the letter A for angstrom, such as 20A and 18A. In 2024 TSMC announced a generation called A16, planned for production in 2026. Like the nanometer names, these are names of generations.
cards.body_zh: 2021 年，英特爾開始用代表埃米的字母 A 替最新幾代製程命名，例如 20A、18A。2024 年，台積電發表了名為 A16 的製程，預計 2026 年生產。和奈米的名字一樣，這些也是世代的名字。

myths.myth_en: A 3-nanometer chip has transistors that are 3 nanometers wide.
myths.myth_zh: 3 奈米晶片裡的電晶體是 3 奈米寬。
myths.fact_en: The 3 is the name of a generation. The closest lines in such a chip are expected to be about 24 nanometers apart.
myths.fact_zh: 3 是這一代的名字。這種晶片裡最密的線，預計相隔大約 24 奈米。

myths.myth_en: So the numbers in chip names mean nothing at all.
myths.myth_zh: 所以晶片名字裡的數字完全沒有意義。
myths.fact_en: They still tell you the order. A smaller number means a newer generation that fits more transistors into the same space.
myths.fact_zh: 它們還是告訴你先後順序：數字越小，代表越新的一代，同樣的面積放得下更多電晶體。

myths.myth_en: A nanometer is the smallest length there is.
myths.myth_zh: 奈米是最小的長度。
myths.fact_en: Atoms are smaller. A silicon atom is about 0.24 nanometers, or 2.4 angstroms, and the parts inside an atom are far smaller still.
myths.fact_zh: 原子更小。矽原子大約 0.24 奈米，也就是 2.4 埃米；原子裡面的東西還要小得多。

myths.myth_en: With a good school microscope you can see viruses and atoms.
myths.myth_zh: 學校的顯微鏡夠好的話，就看得到病毒和原子。
myths.fact_en: A light microscope can only show details down to about 200 nanometers. Viruses, chip lines, and atoms need other kinds of microscopes.
myths.fact_zh: 光學顯微鏡大約只能看清楚 200 奈米以上的細節。病毒、晶片上的線和原子，要用別種顯微鏡才看得到。

tricks.body_en: Each step is a thousand times smaller: millimeter, micrometer, nanometer.
tricks.body_zh: 每一步都小一千倍：公釐（毫米）、微米、奈米。

tricks.body_en: An angstrom is about one atom wide.
tricks.body_zh: 1 埃米大約是一顆原子寬。

tricks.body_en: “3 nanometer” names a generation of chips. Nobody measured 3 nanometers.
tricks.body_zh: 「3 奈米」是一代晶片的名字，沒有人量到 3 奈米。

tricks.body_en: That is about how fast your fingernails grow.
tricks.body_zh: 你的指甲差不多就是長這麼快。

safety.en: Use safety scissors, and cut away from your fingers.
safety.zh: 使用安全剪刀，剪的時候刀口不要對著手指。

safety.en: Do not pull out anyone's hair for the activity. Use a hair that has already fallen out.
safety.zh: 不要為了活動去拔別人的頭髮，用已經掉下來的頭髮就好。

safety.en: Pick up all the tiny pieces of paper when you finish, and keep them away from small children.
safety.zh: 做完之後把小紙屑全部撿起來，不要讓小小孩拿到。

safety.en: If you use a microscope or a magnifying glass, never point it at the sun.
safety.zh: 使用顯微鏡或放大鏡時，絕對不要對著太陽。

activities.title_en: Cut Your Way to a Nanometer

materials.en: A strip of A4 paper cut along the long side (297 millimeters long)
materials.zh: 沿著長邊剪下來的一條 A4 紙（長 297 公釐）

materials.en: Safety scissors, a ruler, and a pencil
materials.zh: 安全剪刀、尺和鉛筆

steps.en: Cut the strip in half. Throw one half away, and cut the other half in half again. Count each cut.
steps.zh: 把紙條對半剪開。丟掉一半，剩下的一半再對半剪。每剪一次就數一次。

steps.en: After each cut, measure the piece and write the length down. How many cuts can you make before the piece is too small to hold?
steps.zh: 每剪一次就量一量、記下長度。剪到第幾次，紙片就小到拿不住了？

steps.en: Keep going with a calculator instead of scissors. After 12 cuts the piece would be as wide as a hair. What is it after 22 cuts?
steps.zh: 接下來不用剪刀，改用計算機繼續算。剪 12 次之後，紙片差不多是一根頭髮寬。剪 22 次之後呢？

steps.en: How many cuts until the piece is shorter than 1 nanometer? Check your answer with the slider on this page.
steps.zh: 要剪幾次，紙片才會短於 1 奈米？用這一頁的滑桿對一對答案。

activities.tip_en: Most people can make only six or seven cuts. The other twenty-two cuts are the distance between what our hands can do and what a chip factory does.
activities.tip_zh: 大部分的人只剪得了六、七次。剩下的二十二次，就是我們的手和晶圓廠之間的距離。

materials.en: Eight cards with these names: fingernail, hair, red blood cell, bacterium, flu virus, chip lines, DNA, silicon atom
materials.zh: 八張卡片，寫上：指甲、頭髮、紅血球、細菌、流感病毒、晶片上的線、DNA、矽原子

materials.en: A long strip of tape on the floor with eight marks, one big step apart
materials.zh: 在地上貼一條長膠帶，上面做八個記號，每個記號相隔一大步

steps.en: Label the marks from 1 centimeter down to 1 angstrom. Each mark is ten times smaller than the one before.
steps.zh: 把記號從 1 公分標到 1 埃米，每個記號都比前一個小十倍。

steps.en: Without looking at the page, put each card where you think it belongs.
steps.zh: 先不要看網頁，把每張卡片放到你覺得對的位置。

steps.en: Check with the 3D model and move the cards that were wrong. Which one surprised you most?
steps.zh: 用 3D 模型對答案，把放錯的卡片移到對的位置。哪一張最讓你意外？

steps.en: Where would you put “3 nanometers”? Is anything on your cards really that size?
steps.zh: 「3 奈米」該放在哪裡？你的卡片裡有哪一樣東西真的是那個大小嗎？

activities.tip_en: On this line, one step is ten times. Three steps are a thousand times, which is one change of unit.
activities.tip_zh: 在這條線上，走一步是十倍；走三步是一千倍，剛好換一個單位。

sources.en: The angstrom is 10⁻¹⁰ m (0.1 nm); named after Anders Jonas Ångström (1814–1874); his 1868 chart of sunlight; never part of the SI; used for atoms and chemical bonds
sources.zh: 埃米是 10⁻¹⁰ 公尺（0.1 奈米）；以埃格斯特朗（1814–1874）命名；1868 年的太陽光譜圖；不屬於 SI；用於原子與化學鍵

sources.zh: nano 代表十億分之一；源自希臘文 nanos「矮人」；1960 年成為正式字首

sources.en: Human hair is 17 to 181 µm in diameter; a nominal value often chosen is 75 µm
sources.zh: 人的頭髮直徑 17–181 微米；常取 75 微米為代表值

sources.en: A red blood cell has a disk diameter of about 6.2–8.2 µm
sources.zh: 紅血球的圓盤直徑約 6.2–8.2 微米

sources.en: E. coli cells are rod-shaped and about 2.0 µm long
sources.zh: 大腸桿菌呈桿狀，長約 2.0 微米

sources.zh: A 型流感病毒直徑 80–120 奈米

sources.zh: 「2 奈米」也一樣；英特爾 2021 年的 20A、18A 命名，A 代表埃米

sources.zh: 台積電 2024 年 4 月 24 日發表 A16 製程，預計 2026 年生產

Silicon: single-bond covalent radius 117.6 pm (so neighboring atoms are about 0.235 nm apart); lattice constant 0.5431 nm

sources.en: Fingernails grow about 3.5 mm a month on average (Yaemsiri and others, 2010)
